subject: gnomeTinkerer
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: gnome tinkerer with a backpack of gadgets.
Style: whimsical low-poly mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning the proportions and skeleton structure for the gnome model, starting with the hips joint and spine chain to build out the rig.

Still defining the skeleton joints...

Configuring the gear train parameters...

I'm sticking with API patterns I know work well — part with geometries, sweep with paths, chain, limb, loft — to avoid pitfalls with less familiar methods.

For the face, simple spheres for eyes with white and pupils feel safer and cuter than decals, and goggles can be made with low-poly torus rings for a glowing lens effect. Now I'm picking the color palette: rosy skin tone, a brighter nose, off-white beard, and leaning toward a classic red for the hat.

I'm settling on a burnt-orange hat with a brass band and gear emblem, mossy green striped tunic, brown pants, dark brown boots with brass buckles, a tan leather apron, dark belt, and leather gloves. For the body I'm building the torso as a swept shape along a spine chain running from hips to chest, varying the radius to give it a pot-bellied silhouette.

Writing torso geometry...

Now I'm working through the spine sweep with catmull-rom knots producing three spans, matching the names array. For the pelvis I'm adding a scaled sphere at the hips for pants, then setting up leg limbs from the hip root to target points with specific lengths, checking that the segment lengths roughly match the hip-to-target distance.

Still writing leg chain code...

Adding the boot cuff and buckle details, checking the sphere geometry bounds so the boot sits flush with the ground, then moving to the arm setup with shoulder joints positioned for a slightly relaxed A-pose stance.

For each hand I'll build five finger chains with two joints apiece, parented to the wrist, giving a simple extended-digit look across both hands.

Working out finger joint positions and thumb placement relative to the hand's local axes, trying to figure out which side corresponds to the palm's inner edge for each arm based on world-space orientation.

Placing the palm box using the hand frame for orientation, positioned slightly above the wrist joint, with dimensions set for width, length along the bone, and thickness. I'll skip elbow cuff rings for now and move toward sleeve geometry for the arm.

For the cuff, I'm using a chain point along the arm at roughly 85% length, treating it as a frame so its tangent sets the cylinder's orientation and bone weighting follows automatically. Now moving to the head: a skin-toned sphere with a prominent nose sphere at the front and rosy cheeks, plus eyes.

For the beard, I'm sketching out a lofted shape hanging from the chin downward, bushy and full-width, bound to the head bone with a few stations defining width and height along its length.

Now I'm placing facial features: a white moustache sweeping from under the nose, defining the head center and scale, positioning the nose as a slightly elongated sphere, and setting eye positions with white spheres and black pupils offset toward the front of the face.

Placing the eyes at azimuth ±24, elevation 8 for symmetry, then figuring out the pupils: sinking small black spheres slightly outward from each eye's surface normal so they sit just proud of the eye socket while staying within the eyeball's radius.

Adjusting the radii so the pupil pokes out slightly from the white eye sphere without exceeding its bounds, then considering a tiny glint sphere offset upward for extra cuteness, though I might skip that detail to keep things simple.

I'm checking my math on where the surface of the head sits at those brow points, realizing my floating offsets are off by a few millimeters, and deciding it's better to place brow hairs by computing actual skin surface hits via azimuth/elevation sampling around the head, then lifting outward from there.

I'll write a small helper that takes azimuth and elevation, finds the surface hit point, and offsets it along the normal by a small lift amount to position hair roots correctly, with a null check in case the ray misses. For the mouth, I'm noting the moustache and beard will cover it anyway, so the gnome's mouth itself can stay simple and small.

Now thinking through the jaw structure: I'll add a jaw bone with joint positioned forward and down, a half-sphere lower jaw piece in skin color, and attach the beard loft to the jaw bone instead of the head so it moves naturally with jaw motion, while the moustache stays on the head bone. I'll skip adding visible tongue/mouth interior detail and just let the upper lip read as part of the head sphere.

Adding mouth and hat shape...

Adding the hat brim geometry...

Defining the hat sweep path...

Adding a red spotted paint pattern to give it a mushroom-gnome look, then placing a small brass gear emblem on the front of the hat band using the gear geometry sized to fit. Now I'm positioning a pair of goggle lenses as torus shapes above the band on the forehead.

I'm checking that the lens discs sit close enough to the curved hat surface at that height — the gap is only about 5mm, which should look fine given the slope, with the glass disc positioned just inside the brass ring's thickness.

For the gnome's ears, I'm using small spike cones extruding from the head at roughly ±85° azimuth, angled outward, back, and up slightly, sized small enough to tuck partially under the hat brim without clipping through it.

Now I'm adding facial details: blush discs as flat cylinders on the cheeks at ±35° azimuth, and a small embedded sphere for the nose near the front center. Then I'm moving to the torso, planning a belt loop wrapped around the hips using a surface cut across the spine bone.

Still working through the belt and buckle placement, considering how to position it relative to the waist joint's frame, before moving on to sketching an apron panel extruded from a front outline.

A flat apron plane would clip into the curved belly, so instead I'll use a decal — an SVG texture of a leather apron with stitching and a pocket with a tool sticking out, conformed onto the torso surface near the belly front with a slight lift to avoid z-fighting.

I'm sketching the SVG: a trapezoid apron shape in tan leather color, darker pocket panels, dashed stitching lines, rivets, and tool handles poking out, sized so stroke widths stay crisp at the render resolution. For suspenders/straps, I'll drape curved paths from the hips over each shoulder to the back using catmull-rom points with a slight lift so they hug the torso naturally.

I'm adding a neckerchief using a flattened torus around the neck for the scarf ring, plus a small knot hanging in front, though I realize the beard likely covers most of it, so I'm trimming the beard to end higher around y .72 so the scarf stays visible.

Now I'm sizing the backpack: a leather-colored box attached to the chest bone, roughly 0.26 wide by 0.34 tall by 0.14 deep, positioned behind the figure, with panel detailing for texture.

Skipping extra straps. For the backpack gadgets, I'm placing a small gear train on the back face of the pack, positioning the big gear and pinion with specific module and tooth counts to get the right pitch and outer diameters relative to the pack's width.

I'm working out the geometry so adjacent gears mesh without overlapping, tracking which pairs are supposed to be connected versus which need a distance check to avoid visual clipping.

Using equal angles keeps everything along a line, so I'm considering adding a fourth gear as a compound gear on the same axle but shifted slightly along the layer axis to avoid meshing collisions, checking that the shift exceeds half the combined thickness for clearance, then attaching a fifth gear off that one and verifying it doesn't loop back and overlap the first gear's layer.

Working out specific gear sizes and placements now—picking tooth counts and pitch diameters for g0 (16 teeth) and g1 (10 teeth), then computing their offset positions so they fit within the pack while respecting symmetry constraints.

Checking layer separation rules — confirming g4's distance from g0 and g1 clears the minimum spacing threshold given their layer differences, so the overlap is visually fine but logically distinct layers.

For the mirrored positions, I'm reasoning that whichever side g1 lands on doesn't matter since g4 stays fixed at 180. For the spin joints, I'm assigning each gear to an axle (g0, g1 with g3, g4) using "gear" spin joints under a pack bone, making sure joint names stay unique across the model before calling spin(20) to set the rest pose.

Now I'm thinking through parts that attach to the chest joint versus the gear joints, and planning the color scheme using the default metal paint cycle. Then I move on to designing a second gadget—a brass telescopic spyglass mounted diagonally on the pack, working out coordinates for its rod and lens-end rings before sketching out a broader list of gadget ideas to add to the pack.

I'm checking whether the spyglass's vertical placement would collide with the figure's arm as it moves, working through the shoulder-to-elbow geometry to avoid overlap, then sketching a few more accessories: a copper horn/funnel lathed into a bell shape on top of the pack, and a pressure gauge dial using a texture on the pack's side face.

Now I'm adding more gear: a wrench and hammer tucked into side loops built from extruded outlines and simple box/cylinder shapes, plus an antenna with a coiled spring and glowing bulb on top. I'm also placing a small glowing lantern hanging from a chain at the figure's left hip, working out its exact attachment point near the belt.

For the pack itself, I'm adding a horizontal copper cylinder tank underneath, like a brass bedroll or boiler with bands, pipe, and valve wheel, then considering a whimsical spinning propeller hat on top made from a mast rod with extruded blades.

I'm attaching that rotor to the chest joint with a parent-dir setup so it can spin for animation, keeping the part count reasonable while adding a side gauge on the pack—a gilt cylindrical dial housing with a glass circle face—positioned on the pack's left face.

Now I'm working out the pack geometry: a box roughly 0.30×0.36×0.14 centered behind the torso, checking it doesn't clash badly with the chest and belly curvature. Since there's a gap between the pack and the upper back, I'm pulling the pack's z-position closer to embed slightly into the belly, accepting minor overlap there while leaving a small gap near the top to be covered by shoulder straps.

Now I'm placing the top flap and vertical back straps with buckles, checking x-coordinates so the straps clear the gear boxes attached nearby, adjusting positions slightly so the strap width doesn't collide with the outer edge of the gears.

Next I'm working out vertical placement for each gear circle based on their centers and outer radii so they fit within the pack's y-span without overlapping the top flap region, then thinking about where to attach the gauge and tool loops with wrench and hammer on the left and right sides of the pack.

Still plotting wrench outline points...

I'm now adding the hammer with its handle and head placed in a side pocket, and deciding to skip extra accessories like a monocle or pencil since the gnome already has goggles. I'm keeping the lantern, belt pouches, and tool loops, then working out how the apron decal texture attaches to the torso surface so it shows below the beard.

I'm checking the apron placement against the torso sweep's hip region — sizing it at height .28 centered around y .53 so it spans roughly .39 to .67, overlapping slightly with the beard but staying within the torso's projectable surface rather than spilling onto the separate pelvis sphere.

Now I'm looking at how the torso's radius profile tapers from hips to chest and realizing the rounded bottom cap extends past the nominal hip boundary down to about y .25, which happens to work out nicely since it makes the tunic read as hanging to mid-thigh, a pleasant gnome-like silhouette rather than a problem to fix.

I'll go with a flat hem at y .36 with a small trim torus to finish the edge, letting legs emerge from underneath with round caps so they tuck naturally into the tunic, and I don't think I need a separate pelvis fill since the hip width comfortably covers the leg radius.

For the spine shape, I'm considering giving the torso a slight forward belly curve by shifting the path along the frame's normal axis—since vertical bones treat +Z as backward, I need a negative shift to push the belly forward using a sine-based offset along the spine's length.

Checking the pack box position relative to the torso back surface, I work out that with the front face around z=−.12 there's a small gap of a few centimeters from the torso, which seems acceptable since straps would bridge that distance. I settle on a pack centered at [0, 0.56, −0.20] with size [0.30, 0.36, 0.16], giving a z-range from −.28 to −.12.

Now I'm placing the gear train behind the pack's back face, layering each gear outward along the z-axis with slight offsets for thickness, and giving the arbor pins a bit of extra length beyond the gear faces. For the spyglass, I'm planning a telescoping design laid across the top of the pack with three tapering sections and a glowing lens at the end.

Checking clearance against the head and shoulders, I decide to angle the spyglass diagonally up and to the left so it clears the head and arm positions, defining it as a series of rod segments with decreasing radius for the telescoping effect.

Now working out the rest of the pack-top arrangement: positioning the spyglass to the left, the rotor mast at x −.09 with blades spanning radius .2 behind the head, and checking clearances so the hat brim, head, and rotor blades don't collide in z and y space.

I also place the antenna on the right at x −.12 with a coil rod from y .76 to 1.0 topped by a glowing bulb, and I'm considering whether to add a copper funnel horn sticking out from the pack's right side near the lantern on the belt.

Instead of that funnel, I'm swapping in a small steam stack arrangement: a cylindrical boiler tank under the pack along the X axis (radius .05, length .30), positioned at y≈.34, z −.2, with gilt end caps and three torus bands. I'll add a small chimney pipe (radius .014, height .06) with a flared lathe top, a pressure valve wheel, and maybe a cluster of cream smoke puffs above it.

Now I'm figuring out where to hang the lantern — off a small loop at the left hip of the belt, positioned around [0.17, 0.30, 0.06], dangling just below the tunic hem near the outer leg line.

The lantern itself I'm building as a small caged cylinder with a glowing orange core, plus a cone cap and base ring with a handle, parented to the hip bone. Skipping belt pouches and hair details, but I'll add boot buckles and maybe eyebrow tufts for character.

Now I'm assigning skeletal roles to each joint — spine, neck, legs, arms, head, jaw, and fingers — keeping the pose a relaxed A-pose rather than strict T-pose.

For the jaw, I'm positioning it under the head with an aim target forward-down, building the lower jaw as a flattened sphere with a beard loft bone attached, and adding a dark interior sphere for the mouth. Then I'm working out the neck chain geometry so it connects cleanly from the torso top up into the head base.

For the head itself, I'm considering a low-poly faceted sphere with flat shading for a crisp cute look, while keeping eyes smooth, and making sure raycasting against the faceted mesh still works fine. I also need to keep the color palette limited to around 40 flat colors to stay under the material limit.

Now I'm setting up the imports I'll need from the SDK—core builder functions plus the glow and clockwork kits—and double-checking the module paths are correct before writing the actual scene code.

Defining the build function and joint hierarchy...

I'm adding the neck chain with two joints plus a head joint aimed outward, then setting up a torso sweep over the spine using a tapered radius array and tunic-striped coloring with ten sides.

For the stripe paint, I decide axis "y" gives horizontal rings since bands vary along y, which looks right for the tunic using green tones, and I note the default axis "z" would ring the body instead. Now I'm starting the leg loop, mirroring left and right limbs symmetrically.

Still writing leg chains...

Adding boot and toe cap geometry...

Confirming scale accepts a vector array, then I'm working out arm geometry—placing shoulder and hand targets and checking elbow distances against limb segment lengths to make sure the joint math stays within reach.

For the elbow bend direction, I'm picking a hint vector that pushes the elbow back and down for a natural bend, then setting up the arm chain with proper joint naming (shoulder, elbow, hand) parented to the chest.

Now I'm adding sleeve geometry with a tapered radius and solid green color, plus cuffs at the forearm, and placing a rounded shoulder pad sphere scaled down at the shoulder joint to match the tunic's smooth look. For hands, I'm planning finger offsets spaced symmetrically along the local axis.

Working out finger joint chains...

Confirming local +X maps to model right, so positive x works for the left-arm inner thumb placement. Now I'm moving to the head: building a skull sphere positioned and scaled against the head bone, wrapping a surface helper around it, and defining an `onHead` function that places features using azimuth/elevation offsets from the head center point.

Adding eye geometry...

Adjusting the pupil direction with a blend toward forward-facing, then working out brow and cheek placements. For the nose, I'm using a small scaled sphere stick near the face center, colored a warm pink. I'm also calculating moustache placement by finding the head surface position just below the nose to anchor curling sweep strokes on either side.

The tip point lands slightly inside the head surface, close enough to work. Now I'm defining beard loft stations with position, width, and height values tapering from the jaw down toward the chin and chest.

I need to check the beard sits properly over the torso front rather than clipping into it — the torso chest front edge is around z≈.135, so I'm nudging the beard stations forward (z values around .10 to .18) and adjusting heights so the beard shell wraps convincingly over the torso rather than embedding inside it.

Adding three beard spike tufts with a small gold bead ring at the end for a whimsical touch, then moving to the hat chain setup, parenting it to the head near the brim with the first joint positioned at the hat base.

For the chain itself I'm tapering radii from thick to thin along five path points curving upward and backward, giving it a hooked sweep. I'm adding a cream-yellow bobble sphere at the tip for a pompom effect, then posing the last joint to droop for a floppy finish.

For the hat's texture I'm adding reddish spots with a cream color scattered sparsely, and building a band as a lathed rectangle profile sitting near the base, colored dark brown leather with a brass buckle accent.

Checking the radius math: the hat's surface width needs to stay inside the band's outer radius while poking slightly through the inner edge, so I'm widening the band profile to [0.115 to 0.15] with no smoothing to keep it from intersecting awkwardly with the hat.

Verifying the head ellipsoid radius near the hat's bottom edge still fits within the band inner radius, and checking that the ears at ±88 degrees sit below the band without clipping. Now I'm positioning the goggles on the hat's sloped surface around y=1.065, checking what the hat radius is at that height.

Working out lens positions and ring geometry...

I'm sketching the goggle glass as a slightly offset glowing circle with a cyan tint, and deciding to skip a gear emblem on the hat since the goggles already occupy that space—though I consider adding a small brass gear below them on the band instead.

Now I'm positioning that gear on the band front, aligning its axle with the band's z-depth so it sits flush with proper inner/outer thickness. Then I move on to the jaw, using a flattened sphere for the lower jaw shape (mostly hidden by beard), skipping teeth, and starting to place a small dark red sphere for the mouth.

I decide the moustache will overlay the mouth anyway, so I skip adding a tongue and keep the smile minimal since it'll be mostly hidden. For the belt, I work out which spine joint to anchor it to—settling on spine2 near y=.48 rather than spine1—and plan to loop skin geometry through that joint point with a slight lift.

Now I'm getting the torso surface, finding the loop point for the belt, and placing a brass buckle box in front of it, oriented so its short dimension points outward along the surface normal.

Next I'm adding two leather pouches positioned at side angles on the belt, sizing them roughly cube-shaped with outward-facing thickness, then capping each with a small cylindrical flap bulging outward to mimic a pouch cover.

Now I'm confirming the apron decal hits the torso surface correctly rather than the arms, then sketching the apron's SVG shape with a tapered neck strap and polygon outline matching the decal's aspect ratio.

Adding pocket and tool details...

Then I move to the backpack, placing a leather box on the chest bone with panelled paint for rivets. A simple box shape should work fine even if blocky, since the paint texture handles the detail.

Adding flap and side pockets...

Now I'm positioning the gears centered near x=0 within range, then adding a pressure gauge on the left pocket face—a cylindrical housing with a glass dial using a gauge texture, placed at the pocket's vertical center so it fits within the pocket height, oriented to face outward along +X with the dial upright.

Moving on to the spyglass, rotor, antenna, tank, and lantern details: I'm defining a rotor joint on the chest at a specific offset with a hinge-like role, connecting it with a brass mast rod, then building a hub sphere and two blade extrusions for the rotor.

Still writing blade geometry...

I'll add three blades rotated around the hub at 120-degree intervals, computing perpendicular axes for each so the thickness stays consistent, then color them with a copper metal paint. I'll place the rotor at the joint position with slight y-offsets for blade thickness, then move on to positioning the antenna on the right side.

For the rotor mount, I'll center it at x=0, raised near the top of the head and set back behind the head's centerline, checking that the blade radius clears the head's back edge. To avoid collision with the spyglass resting diagonally across the top, I'll shift the spyglass slightly left, verifying the gap between its radius and the mast radius stays positive.

Checking blade sweep height against the spyglass tip confirms clearance, so that placement works. For the antenna, I'm positioning it on the opposite side with a coiled spring shape around a thin steel rod, topped with a small glowing sphere, then double-checking it doesn't overlap the rotor blade's swept radius.

Lowering the antenna top so the bulb clears the blade sweep works out, with the mast extended slightly and the bulb kept well below the blade's bottom edge. Now I'm checking the spyglass clearance against the rotor hub, then moving on to the tank geometry under the pack, setting up a horizontal cylinder oriented along the X axis for its placement.

Positioning the tank clear of the tunic hem and legs, I'm checking it doesn't collide front or back, then painting it copper with verdigris. Now I'm adding decorative torus bands along the tank's length, figuring out the axis orientation, and sketching small end-cap cylinders for gilt rims plus a torus valve wheel on top.

Working out the lantern placement on the left hip, checking it clears the hanging arm and elbow, and sketching a chain rod connecting it to the belt.

Now I'm building the lantern itself with a hexagonal glowing body, a brass-colored top cone, bottom disc, and a small handle ring, attached near the hips bone where the belt sits against the torso.

I'm also adding a scarf torus at the neck and considering a cross-body bandolier strap.

Working out the vial placement on the belt...

Mapping out which belt arc is front versus sides, I place the vials symmetrically flanking the belly decal using small slices near the front arc, and I'm working out how to orient the vials vertically against the belt's tangent-based frame rather than along it.

Building the vial geometry with a cylindrical body, glass-colored glow, and a small cork cap, then positioning each one at its belt point lifted slightly upward so it stands off the surface instead of embedding into it.

Adding brass corks to six vials total, then setting gear poses to spin at 15 degrees. For gnome whimsy I'm adding small white spiky hair tufts near the ears beneath the hat, keeping it to one per side. I'm also double-checking that I only import the names actually used, since unused imports could trip up the TS typecheck.

Starting the build function with vector helpers and color constants...

Now I'm setting up the skeleton: hips joint as root, a spine chain built with catmull-rom control points, then referencing the third spine joint as the chest. I'm building the torso as a tapered sweep along the spine with a slight sine-based offset for a natural curve.

Adding the hem trim torus geometry at the hip base, then moving on to legs, head, and a neck sweep, verifying each API call matches the expected parameters as I go.

I'm figuring out the scarf torus placement — it sits partly inside the torso radius so I'll bump its size up slightly, decide the beard covers the front enough to skip back-hanging scarf tails, and sketch the suspender straps as a draped sweep path.

Now I'm mirroring the straps to both sides, looping through the arm/glove geometry, and placing ear spikes anchored to the head bone with a surface-hit base. Then I'm adding small white beard-colored hair tufts near the temples, angled outward and tucked under the hat band.

I'm checking that the hat brim height clips the tuft position correctly, settling on a lower elevation angle so they poke out visibly. Now I'm working through the remaining props in order: hat construction, goggles, pack, then composing everything together, while confirming the part/rod helper signatures for the gear and spyglass pieces.

For the spyglass, I'm adding tiny torus rings at section junctions oriented along the rod direction, using small glow lenses made from circle geometry, and starting the leather grip section with brass accent rings at the ends. Now I'm setting up the gear train configuration with its position, axis, module size, and bone attachment before defining the individual gears.

Still writing gear specs...

I'm double-checking the gear chain references—gear 2 mounts onto gear 1 with a shift and copper verdigris coloring, gear 3 derives from gear 2 at an opposite angle—then verifying the spin animation and default up-axis behavior work correctly with the chosen axis direction, plus checking the spoke count condition for the first gear's rim thickness.

Checking the gap condition for holes on g2: rim minus hub clearance exceeds twice the module, so holes apply—I'll set holes to 5 for g2 since spokes aren't triggered there. For g1 with 10 teeth, the pitch is small enough that a solid disc works fine, and positioning relative to g0 at 40° gives offsets of roughly ±.0668 in x. Now moving to g3, placed at 180° from gear index 2 with a distance of .056.

I'm checking that the top and bottom edges of the gears stay within the packing bounds, confirming layer separation is sufficient for the remaining axle pairs so none of them require collision checks, and verifying thickness values default correctly to .016 for each gear.

For the arbor radius, I'm taking the minimum of bore (or infinity if undefined) and 55% of hub size, checking that this resolves fine even when g3 has no bore defined. I'm also reviewing the joint setup, confirming the chest bone parents the spin joints at each gear's axle position correctly, and that pose and gauge texture calls look fine overall — just minor rig concerns remain.

Now I'm tallying up the color palette across the whole figure — skin tones, hat details, straps, leather, tunic, boots, trim, glove, scarf, wood, steel, and glow colors — landing around thirty flat colors total, which seems reasonable. I'm also making sure the TypeScript stays strict by avoiding implicit any types as I define the onHead helper.

Writing hit detection logic...

I'm figuring out how the sphere's around() method casts rays from a center point to find surface hits, confirming that a ray along +Z from center lands on the front of the head. Then I'm deriving brow points from several hit coordinates, building a lifted() helper that offsets a point along its normal by a given amount, and deciding the moustache can just use fixed points since precision isn't critical there.

Now I'm adding goggles geometry: torus rims and glowing lens circles positioned symmetrically on each side of the head, oriented along a tilted forward direction, plus a cylindrical rim tube behind each lens.

I'm sweeping the strap ring as a tube and checking that its radius and z-offset match the hat surface at that height, confirming the hat is hollow above the head so the strap sits correctly against the brim.

Now I'm typing out the accessory outlines—annotating the wrench and rotor blade shapes as explicit tuple arrays so TypeScript infers them correctly—then building the hammer with a wooden rod handle and starting its head geometry.

I'm checking that the hammer's handle and head sit properly within the tool pocket, verifying x and z coordinates align with the pocket's bounds before moving on to the right pocket's box dimensions.

Still adding pack details...

Now I'm adding the clasp position relative to the flap, checking the shoulder straps connect correctly from the torso down into the pack front, and then writing hand geometry attached to each arm's last joint, positioned slightly offset from the hand bone.

Adding finger joints...

Totaling joint counts gets me to roughly 48 with fingers, gears, and rotor included. I'm checking the hat chain setup with its bobble sphere attached to the tip joint, then sweeping the hat shape with tapering radii and a pointed cap. Now I'm working out the cuff band using a lathe shape...

I'm also sanity-checking proportions: boot soles and feet stay just above y=0, and the overall height with the hat bobble lands around 1.3 meters — bigger than folklore gnomes but reasonable for a cartoon tinkerer character.

Next I'm building the lantern cone on the hip bone, then working out the belt loop for the vials: sweeping a cylindrical belt around the hip, slicing two arcs for the vial placements, and positioning each vial radially outward from the spine center using a normalized direction vector. I'm defining the vial geometry as a small cylinder.

Now I'm adding corks on top of each vial, assigning colors from a palette array, and applying a glow effect to each part. Then I'm starting the SVG path for the apron shape with a tan fill and dark stroke outline.

Writing SVG path...

Still writing SVG code...

Deciding to skip scaling the nose and keep it simple, then moving on to finalize the lantern chain rod attached to the hips bone, and setting up a side variable to distinguish left/right in the loop before importing the glow utility.

Now checking the typing for joints, frame parameters, and bone omission on sticks, then assembling the spyglass rods with proper color and bone attachments, confirming rod end caps render as torus rings, and setting up the tank's cylinder geometry before writing the final answer.
